C3-09-L01 - Capstone ADR: business problem, architecture and
non-functional requirements
Focused effort: 2.5 h | RetailPulse checkpoint P01 | Review R01 locked until attempt saved
1. Why it matters
A capstone proves integration and ownership. A disconnected demo or copied snippet is weaker than a smaller coherent system with
explicit requirements, failure boundaries and independent validation.
2. What you learn
Start RetailPulse from business users, data products, freshness, recovery, integrity, security, cost and operability - not from a tool checklist.
3. Prerequisite
C3-08 Gate PASS and retained evidence from C3-00 through C3-08. Use the prior verified tool environment for any live
Airflow/Spark/dbt/Fabric/Kafka work; new concepts in this lesson are still explained here.
4. Picture it in your head
Picture a house plan drawn before buying appliances. The ADR states who lives there, what must work, what can fail, and why one layout
was chosen. Tools come after the requirements.
5. New words before we use them
ADR = Architecture Decision Record. Functional requirement = what the system must do. NFR = measurable quality requirement such as
freshness, recovery, security or cost. Trade-off = benefit accepted with a cost/constraint.
6. Useful video/source
CURRENT REFERENCE - Azure Well-Architected Framework
Why use it: Architecture/NFR/trade-off framing. Segment: whole relevant page.
OPTIONAL VISUAL - John Savill - Microsoft Fabric Overview
Why use it: Optional platform architecture orientation. Segment: Use architecture/platform overview; current docs control behavior..
7. Plain-English explanation
An Architecture Decision Record records context, measurable requirements, considered options, decision, consequences and rejected
alternatives. A strong capstone can justify a simpler batch-first design when daily freshness is sufficient.

8. Tiny worked example
RetailPulse needs daily trusted sales by 09:00, one failed day recoverable independently, no secrets in Git, and low idle cost. A batch-first
design can satisfy this; Kafka would add complexity without a sub-minute consumer.
9. Follow with me once
Open docs/ADR_001_RETAILPULSE_TODO.md. Write users/data products first, then measurable
freshness/recovery/integrity/security/cost NFRs, compare batch-first with one alternative, and record the decision/consequence.
10. Expected result
ADR names users/data products, measurable NFRs, at least two options, chosen design, rejected alternative and consequences. Tool
names are secondary to requirements.
11. Why it worked
The checkpoint has an explicit requirement, input/output grain or resource boundary, a deterministic success condition and a separate
validation path. The result is accepted because the evidence agrees with the contract - not merely because a command returned exit code
12. Break / fix / debug
If the ADR says only which tools you like, restate the consumer outcome and failure budget before choosing architecture.
13. Common beginner mistakes
• Starting with Kafka/Spark/Fabric names before writing the business outcome.
• Writing vague NFRs such as "fast" or "secure".
• Listing one option only, so no decision was actually made.

C3-09-L02 - Source contracts, synthetic/public data and
reproducible inputs
Focused effort: 2.5 h | RetailPulse checkpoint P02 | Review R02 locked until attempt saved
1. Why it matters
A capstone proves integration and ownership. A disconnected demo or copied snippet is weaker than a smaller coherent system with
explicit requirements, failure boundaries and independent validation.
2. What you learn
Define source grain, stable keys, timestamps, schema, ownership and allowed change while keeping the project reproducible without
employer/private data.
3. Prerequisite
C3-08 Gate PASS and retained evidence from C3-00 through C3-08. Use the prior verified tool environment for any live
Airflow/Spark/dbt/Fabric/Kafka work; new concepts in this lesson are still explained here.
4. Picture it in your head
Picture each source as a sealed parcel with a label: one row means what, which field is the identity, when it changed, who owns it, and what
changes are allowed. The contract is that label.
5. New words before we use them
Grain = what one row/event represents. Stable key = identity used across changes. Change timestamp/version = ordering signal for
updates. Contract = declared schema/semantics/ownership/compatibility. Synthetic data = safe generated data that represents patterns
without private records.
6. Useful video/source
CURRENT REFERENCE - dbt model contracts
Why use it: Contract guarantees and breaking-change thinking. Segment: Why define a contract + breaking changes.
7. Plain-English explanation
A capstone is stronger when another reviewer can rerun it from safe public/synthetic inputs. Versioned source contracts separate source
truth from assumptions and make late corrections, schema drift and historical replay explicit.

C3-09-L03 - Build the batch ingestion path
Focused effort: 3.0 h | RetailPulse checkpoint P03 | Review R03 locked until attempt saved
1. Why it matters
A capstone proves integration and ownership. A disconnected demo or copied snippet is weaker than a smaller coherent system with
explicit requirements, failure boundaries and independent validation.
2. What you learn
Land source-preserving evidence with run metadata and prove a repeat of the same batch is safe.
3. Prerequisite
C3-08 Gate PASS and retained evidence from C3-00 through C3-08. Use the prior verified tool environment for any live
Airflow/Spark/dbt/Fabric/Kafka work; new concepts in this lesson are still explained here.
4. Picture it in your head
Picture a loading dock with an untouched receiving area and a separate inspected shelf. Landing preserves what arrived; trusted current
state is published only after validation. Replaying the same delivery must not duplicate business state.
5. New words before we use them
Landing = source-preserving intake. Bronze = raw/replay layer. Run ID = identity for one execution. Hash = deterministic fingerprint of bytes.
Idempotent = repeating the same logical operation converges to the same business state.
6. Useful video/source

Why use it: Current standard-library CSV behavior used by the local proof. Segment: reader/writer/DictReader sections.
7. Plain-English explanation
Batch ingestion should preserve the original source sample, record a deterministic file hash/run identity and separate landing evidence from
validated current state. Rerunning an unchanged source must not silently duplicate logical output.

C3-09-L04 - Add incremental / CDC-style change handling
Focused effort: 3.0 h | RetailPulse checkpoint P04 | Review R04 locked until attempt saved
1. Why it matters
A capstone proves integration and ownership. A disconnected demo or copied snippet is weaker than a smaller coherent system with
explicit requirements, failure boundaries and independent validation.
2. What you learn
Apply corrections/new records deterministically with stable key and update semantics, then prove each logical change occurs once.
3. Prerequisite
C3-08 Gate PASS and retained evidence from C3-00 through C3-08. Use the prior verified tool environment for any live
Airflow/Spark/dbt/Fabric/Kafka work; new concepts in this lesson are still explained here.
4. Picture it in your head
Picture a bookmark plus correction slips. The bookmark tells you how far you processed, while each correction is tied to a stable business
key and change time. Advancing the bookmark before safe publish risks losing changes.
5. New words before we use them
Incremental load = process only new/changed input. High-water mark = progress boundary. CDC = change data capture. Upsert/MERGE =
insert new keys and update matching keys. Replay = reapply historical input. Tie-break = deterministic rule when versions tie.
6. Useful video/source
CURRENT REFERENCE - Debezium 3.6 documentation
Why use it: CDC change-event semantics and durable ordering context. Segment: What is it + connector/tutorial concepts.
OPTIONAL VISUAL - freeCodeCamp - Apache Kafka for Beginners
Why use it: Optional topics/partitions/producers/consumers visual before CDC integration. Segment: Use modern concepts; current Debezium/Kafka docs control exact
behavior..
7. Plain-English explanation
Incremental correctness requires more than a watermark. You need a stable key, authoritative change timestamp/version rule, deterministic
conflict policy and reconciliation. Late corrections can invalidate simplistic max-timestamp polling assumptions.

C3-09-L07 - Orchestration, retries, backfills and partial reruns
Focused effort: 3.5 h | RetailPulse checkpoint P07 | Review R07 locked until attempt saved
1. Why it matters
A capstone proves integration and ownership. A disconnected demo or copied snippet is weaker than a smaller coherent system with
explicit requirements, failure boundaries and independent validation.
2. What you learn
Coordinate the capstone by data interval, classify transient versus deterministic failures and prove bounded historical reprocessing.
3. Prerequisite
C3-08 Gate PASS and retained evidence from C3-00 through C3-08. Use the prior verified tool environment for any live
Airflow/Spark/dbt/Fabric/Kafka work; new concepts in this lesson are still explained here.
4. Picture it in your head
Picture a train timetable. Airflow coordinates when each carriage moves, but each task must remain safe if the scheduler retries or replays
one interval. Backfill is a bounded historical service, not "rerun everything."
5. New words before we use them
DAG = directed acyclic graph of tasks. Data interval = logical time window a run owns. Retry = repeat after eligible failure. Backfill =
intentional historical processing. Partial rerun = rerun only affected work. Failure class = transient vs deterministic/permanent.

7. Plain-English explanation
Orchestration should make dependencies, interval identity, retries, backfills and partial reruns explicit. A retry is safe only when the
underlying task is idempotent. Historical reprocessing must target a bounded interval without corrupting other dates.
